title: Leveling the Playing Field -- Ch. 8: The Judiciary and Media: Natural Partners in Our Democracy
keywords: The Judiciary and Media: Natural Partners in Our Democracy
Asian Institute of Journalism and Communication
the Supreme Court as a fortress
primary_topics: Chapter 8 of 'Leveling the Playing Field' -- CJP's remarks to a gathering of journalists at the Asian Institute of Journalism and Communication, tracing how the Supreme Court has moved from being 'a fortress - high-walled, forbidding and impenetrable' toward transparency and engagement with media.

The caveat that accompanies that openness: unlike the political branches, the Court issues decisions 'not reversible by elections and referendums,' so once it rules it should not debate with litigants or the gallery -- it welcomes fair criticism but not public debates designed to overturn its judgments.

The case for partnership: judges and journalists share the same raison d'être -- the search for truth, the protection of basic rights and the defense of society's fundamental norms -- and both depend on retaining the public's confidence and on the persuasive power of language and reason.
sub_topics: He notes that it has become 'increasingly common for magistrates to participate in seminars like this' in an age of information and transparency, thanking Dr. Florangel Rosario-Braid for the invitation.

He recalls the old Court as a fortress and a Mount Olympus whose 'gods of Padre Faura' were mysterious, unapproachable and untouchable, speaking in guarded legalese that nonetheless determined the freedom, fame and fortune of those below, and whose decisions no one dared question.

He describes the change: the doors have been unlocked and slightly opened, the enclave punctured by the transparency requirements of the Constitution, the Ethical Standards Law and the Canons of Judicial Ethics, while media have 'persistently knocked at the ramparts' until their invasive power penetrated the judicial fortress.

He enumerates the Court's responses -- a Public Information Office under its Committee on Public Information, a web page, more reader-friendly decisions, occasional communion with media, the bulletins Benchmark and Court News, and an interactive radio program by the court administrator.

He explains why the Court still needs media: though it decides strictly on the facts and the law regardless of what the gallery cheers for, it can prevail only with 'long-term public confidence in its probity and good faith.'

He sets the limit: the political departments are subject to endless public debate and periodic popular judgment, but the Court's job is 'to decide legal disputes with finality,' and litigations must end somewhere -- in our system, with the Supreme Court.

He closes with a plea that the seminar help engender 'an informed public appreciation of the judiciary and the rule of law,' not through blind faith but through thoughtful evaluation of the Court as 'the last bulwark of democracy and the final recourse of the damned.'

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 8 of 'Leveling the Playing Field' gathers CJP's short remarks to a gathering of journalists convened by Dr. Florangel Rosario-Braid of the Asian Institute of Journalism and Communication. He began by observing that in an age of information and transparency it had become increasingly common for magistrates to join such seminars, and contrasted that with the distant past, when the Supreme Court was a fortress, high-walled, forbidding and impenetrable, likened to a Mount Olympus where the gods of Padre Faura resided in lofty perches far above the valley dwellers, mysterious and untouchable, speaking only in guarded legalese that nonetheless determined the freedom, fame and fortune of the multitude below. That fortress, he said, had since been unlocked and slightly opened, punctured by the transparency requirements of the Constitution, the Ethical Standards Law and the Canons of Judicial Ethics, and by media practitioners who persistently knocked at its ramparts until their invasive power penetrated its thick walls. In response the Court had created a Public Information Office under its Committee on Public Information, opened a web page, issued more reader-friendly decisions, allowed its members to commune with media, published the bulletins Benchmark and Court News, and authorized an interactive radio program. He added a caveat: unlike the political departments, whose actions face endless debate and periodic popular judgment, the Court issues decisions not reversible by elections or referendums, and its job is to decide legal disputes with finality, so while it is not averse to fair criticism it will not join debates meant to overturn its judgments. He closed by naming the commonalities between judges and journalists -- the search for truth, the protection of basic rights, the defense of society's fundamental norms, and dependence on public confidence -- and asked the seminar to foster informed appreciation of the Court as the last bulwark of democracy and the final recourse of the damned.
